extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Determining who qualifies as a joint inventor for a U.S. patent application under 35 U.S.C. §116, plus how to handle omitted inventors, corrections, and ownership consequences. Covers the legal standard (conception), practical non-inventor scenarios, and risks from misjoinder or omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint application and oath requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention is made by two or more persons jointly, they shall apply for patent jointly and each make the required oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants who qualify as joint inventors must be named on the application and each must execute the required oath/declaration. This establishes a baseline procedural requirement for joint inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in recognizing joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors may apply for a patent jointly even though they did not physically work together or at the same time; each did not make the same type or amount of contribution; or each did not make a contribution to the subject matter of every claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint inventorship is not limited by contemporaneous collaboration, equal contribution, or contribution to every claim — disparate, asynchronous, or partial contributions can still support joint inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling omitted or refusing inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a joint inventor refuses to join in an application or cannot be found or reached after diligent effort, the application may be made by the other inventor on behalf of himself and the omitted inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an inventor is omitted because they refuse or are unreachable after diligent effort, another inventor may file on their behalf. The Director may grant a patent to the applicant subject to the same rights the omitted inventor would have had—practical steps should document diligent effort to locate/secure participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventor standard — conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who shares in the conception of a claimed invention is a joint inventor of that invention; each joint inventor must contribute in some significant manner to the conception of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dispositive legal standard is contribution to conception (the mental act of formulating the invention). Contributions must be significant to conception, not trivial or purely administrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception vs. reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the mental act of formulating the invention (the heart of inventorship); reduction to practice (constructing/testing) alone does NOT confer inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performing experiments, building prototypes, or reducing an idea to practice without contributing to the conception does not make someone an inventor. Mere assistance in reduction to practice, without conception, is not inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workers following instructions are not inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding workers who only followed instructions does NOT make them inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technicians, lab staff, or others who merely execute tasks per directions, without contributing to the inventive conception, should not be named as inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting a goal without a solution is not inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggesting a general goal or problem, but not the solution, does NOT make one an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions that state a purpose, objective, or problem without contributing to the concrete conception or solution do not satisfy the inventorship standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to a single dependent claim may confer inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributing to a single dependent claim can make a person an inventor in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a contribution limited to subject matter of one dependent claim can qualify, depending on whether that contribution meaningfully participates in the conception of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution limited to obvious aspects is not inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing only in obvious aspects of the invention does NOT make one an inventor of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the contribution is limited to elements that would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill and did not partake in inventive conception, inventorship is not established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of inventorship (35 U.S.C. §256)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship can be corrected in issued patents without deceptive intent, by application of all parties or by court order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 256 provides mechanisms to fix inventorship errors post-issuance provided there was no deceptive intent; corrections typically require joint application or judicial action, and practitioners should follow statutory procedures and document intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct risk from deceptive misjoinder/omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Misjoinder or omission of an inventor with deceptive intent can render a patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to properly include or excluding inventors with deceptive intent creates the risk of unenforceability for inequitable conduct; exercise diligence in identifying inventors and avoid intentional omissions or misjoinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent ownership vs. inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors own a patent equally and can each license it independently absent contractual transfer (35 U.S.C. §262); employers typically own through assignment agreements or hired-to-invent doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming inventors establishes ownership interests unless there are assignment agreements or employment-to-invent arrangements transferring rights; practitioners should ensure assignments and agreements are in place to reflect intended ownership and licensing rights.
